newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Canada to appoint salmon troubleshooters.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Canada to appoint salmon troubleshooters.

text.p: The United States and Canada agreed on Wednesday to appoint special troubleshooters to untangle a bitter dispute over the Pacific salmon catch and restart talks on fishing rights.

Canadian Foreign Minister Lloyd Axworthy said he had accepted a U.S. proposal that each country name an "eminent person" whose job would be to reinvigorate the negotiations which stalled last month and led to a confrontation at sea.

Axworthy also told reporters following urgent talks with U.S. Deputy Secretary of State Strobe Talbott that Washington and Ottawa had agreed to open "an early warning communications system" under which U.S. and Canadian officials would stay in daily contact to avert such incidents.

The emergency talks, requested by Axworthy, came after Canadian fishermen had held an Alaskan ferry captive for three days in Prince Rupert, British Columbia, to back their protest against alleged U.S. overfishing.
"We need to lower the temperature of what has been going on ... we have to set the proper climate to resolve our differences and get negotiations back on track as soon as possible," Axworthy said.
The two envoys, yet to be named, will report directly to President Bill Clinton and Prime Minister Jean Chretien.
In Canada, Chretien said on Wednesday he saw no need at the moment to discuss the salmon issue with Clinton.

He said that despite U.S. rejection of arbitration, Ottawa was willing to pursue any diplomatic way of reaching agreement. "If there is anything that is put forward that will lead to a solution, we'll be there," he told reporters.
As the two countries inched closer to resuming the talks, each expressed a desire to move away from the acrimony of the past few days.
"Both sides are looking at a way to get to negotiations. We are looking at a facilitating mechanism that would be a step toward this," State Department spokesman James Foley told reporters earlier.

Long and stormy negotiations between Canadian and U.S officials on how to divide this year's Pacific salmon catch broke down last month. U.S. officials denied breaching any international agreements and blamed Canada for the collapse.
Foley and Axworthy called the hour-long State Department meeting "very good and friendly" and said each side had agreed on the importance of saving the Pacific Salmon accord.
Canadian fishermen have given the Ottawa government one week to make progress on resolving the dispute and have threatened further action if it failed to do so.
The three-day blockade of the Alaskan passenger ferry Malaspina escalated the festering salmon squabble and threatened to damage relations between the United States and its biggest trading partner.
Sen. Frank Murkowski, an Alaska Republican, and other lawmakers have urged retaliation, including using U.S. Navy or Coast Guard vessels to protect Alaskan ferries sailing through Canadian waters.

Murkowski, along with Republican Sens. Ted Stevens of Alaska and Slade Gorton of Washington State, introduced a resolution on Wednesday condemning the Canadian government "for failing to accept responsibility" for the blockade and calling on Clinton to take action.
The non-binding resolution passed the Senate by a vote of 81-19.
